blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 20 (Medical Physics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define radiation and classify it into ionizing and non-ionizing radiation. Give the examples used in medical physics, state how each kind interacts with matter, and describe the medical uses of gamma rays, X-rays, ultrasonic waves and radiowaves. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Radiation: the transfer of energy through space or matter in the form of waves or particles. In medical physics it is mainly used for diagnosis (imaging) and treatment.

Classification:
(i) Ionizing radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions. Examples: X-rays, gamma rays and positrons. X-rays and gamma rays interact with matter through the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering; positrons are emitted from radioactive tracers.
(ii) Non-ionizing radiation does not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms. Examples: ultrasound waves and radiowaves. These waves are reflected, refracted or absorbed when they interact with matter.

Medical uses:
• X-rays: commonly used to image bones and internal organs.
• Gamma rays: used in nuclear medicine, such as PET scans, and in cancer treatment, due to their high penetrating power.
• Ultrasonic waves: ultrasound imaging of soft tissues, monitoring the fetus and studying internal organs safely, without ionizing radiation.
• Radiowaves: used in MRI, where they interact with atomic nuclei to give detailed images of internal structures, especially soft tissues, without harmful radiation exposure.

book_ref.quote: In medical physics, radiation is mainly used for diagnosis (imaging) and treatment.

blocks.prompt: 2 Compare the energy of one photon of X-rays of wavelength 2.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m with that of one photon of the 64 MHz radiowaves used in an MRI scanner. Express both in joules and electronvolts and find their ratio (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Photon energy is E = hc/λ for the X-ray and E = hf for the radiowave; the huge difference explains why one ionizes and the other does not.

book_ref.quote: Non-ionizing radiation does not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms.

blocks.final_answer: X-ray photon ≈ 9.95 × 10⁻¹⁵ J (62 keV); radiowave photon ≈ 4.24 × 10⁻²⁶ J (2.65 × 10⁻⁷ eV); the X-ray photon carries about 2.3 × 10¹¹ times more energy, which is why X-rays are ionizing and radiowaves are not.

blocks.prompt: 3 What is the piezoelectric effect? Give the origin of the name and its discovery, explain the effect in terms of the internal structure of the crystal, distinguish the direct and converse effects, and explain how this effect lets an ultrasound transducer play a dual role. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Name and discovery: "piezoelectric" comes from the Greek "piezein", meaning "to press", and "electric", the production of electricity. The effect was discovered in 1880 by Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie, who found that mechanical pressure on crystals such as quartz, tourmaline and Rochelle salt (sodium potassium tartrate) generated an electric charge, a strong connection between mechanical force and electrical response.

Explanation: the effect is possible because of the unique internal structure of some crystals. These crystals have no centre of symmetry, and inside them there are small regions of positive and negative charge. Normally these charges are balanced. When pressure is applied the balance is disturbed, the charges move slightly, and an electric field appears on the surface (Fig. 20.1, crystal of lead zirconate titanate, PZT).

Two types:
(i) Direct piezoelectric effect: mechanical pressure on the crystal produces an electric field (voltage) on its surface.
(ii) Converse piezoelectric effect: an electric field applied to the crystal makes it change shape a little.
So the effect turns pressure into voltage and vice versa.

Ultrasound transducer: ultrasound imaging operates on this effect, which is central to the transducer. The transducer plays a dual role: it generates the ultrasound waves (its crystal changes shape when a voltage is applied) and then, in receive mode, it detects the reflected echoes, which press on the crystal and are converted into electrical signals by the direct piezoelectric effect.

book_ref.quote: The piezoelectric effect is possible because of the unique internal structure of some crystals.

blocks.prompt: 4 A piezoelectric transducer produces ultrasound of frequency 4.0 MHz. Using v = fλ, find the wavelength of this ultrasound (i) in soft tissue, where sound travels at 1540 m s⁻¹ (ii) in bone, where it travels at 4080 m s⁻¹. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the vibrating crystal; the wavelength changes with the speed in each tissue: λ = v/f.

book_ref.quote: On the other hand, if we apply an electric field to the crystal, it changes shape a little.

blocks.final_answer: (i) 0.385 mm in soft tissue (ii) 1.02 mm in bone.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the physical principles on which diagnostic ultrasound imaging works, from the emission of a pulse to the formation of the image. Why is ultrasound considered a safe and repeatable method? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ultrasound lets doctors view internal body structures in real time (ultrasound machine, Fig. 20.2). Its working is based on these principles:

(i) Emission: a piezoelectric transducer sends pulses of high frequency sound, typically 1 MHz-15 MHz, into the body.
(ii) Travel: the waves travel at different speeds depending on the type of tissue they pass through.
(iii) Reflection: when the waves meet a boundary between two tissues with different acoustic impedances (determined by tissue density and sound speed), part of the wave is reflected as an echo.
(iv) Detection: the transducer switches to receive mode and detects the reflected waves using the direct piezoelectric effect; the echoes are converted into electrical signals and processed by the machine.
(v) Image formation: a computer calculates the time delay and intensity of the returning echoes and constructs a visual image. Areas with stronger reflections appear brighter, revealing internal structures of organs and tissues.

Safety: ultrasound does not use ionizing radiation, so it is a safe, non-invasive and repeatable imaging method.

book_ref.quote: The functioning of ultrasound imaging is based on several physical principles.

blocks.prompt: 6 An ultrasound pulse is sent into the abdomen. Echoes from the front and back walls of an organ return after 65 μs and 91 μs. Taking the speed of sound in tissue as 1540 m s⁻¹, find (i) the depth of the front wall (ii) the depth of the back wall (iii) the thickness of the organ. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The measured time is for the trip to the boundary and back, so depth = vt/2.

book_ref.quote: Finally, a computer calculates the time delay and intensity of the returning echoes to construct a visual image.

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain the factors that affect the quality of an ultrasound image. Also describe the uses of ultrasound in obstetrics, the abdomen, cardiology, urology and the musculoskeletal system. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Factors affecting image quality:
(i) Acoustic impedance difference: a higher difference between two tissues (e.g. soft tissue and bone) causes stronger echoes, producing clearer boundaries in the image.
(ii) Frequency of ultrasound: higher frequency ultrasound gives better resolution but less penetration; lower frequency waves penetrate deeper but give lower image clarity.
(iii) Use of gel: a special gel is applied between the transducer and the skin to remove air gaps and improve transmission of the sound waves.
Ultrasound can also measure blood flow speed using the Doppler effect, by detecting shifts in sound frequency.

Applications:
• Obstetrics: monitoring fetal growth, estimating gestational age and identifying abnormalities during pregnancy.
• Abdomen: examining the liver, kidneys, gallbladder, pancreas and bladder.
• Cardiology: echocardiography evaluates the heart's structure and function in real time.
• Urology: examining the prostate, testicles and urinary system.
• Musculoskeletal system: detecting ligament injuries, joint inflammation and other soft tissue conditions.

book_ref.quote: Acoustic Impedance Difference: A higher difference between two tissues

blocks.prompt: 8 A clinic has probes of 2.0 MHz and 12 MHz. Taking the speed of sound in tissue as 1540 m s⁻¹, find (i) the wavelength of each in tissue (ii) the ratio of the two wavelengths. State which probe suits a deep organ and which gives finer detail near the surface. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use λ = v/f; higher frequency means shorter wavelength, better resolution and less penetration.

book_ref.quote: lower frequency waves penetrate deeper but have lower image clarity

steps: Lower frequency (2.0 MHz) penetrates deeper; higher frequency (12 MHz) gives better resolution but less penetration
blocks.final_answer: (i) 0.77 mm and 0.128 mm (ii) 6.0; use 2.0 MHz for a deep organ and 12 MHz for fine detail near the surface.

blocks.prompt: 9 Explain why electron transitions in light elements give infrared, visible or ultraviolet lines while inner-shell transitions in heavy atoms give X-rays. What are characteristic X-rays and why has their study been important? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Light elements: transitions of electrons in hydrogen or other light elements result in spectral lines in the infrared, visible or ultraviolet region, because the energy differences between the transition levels are small.

Heavy atoms: the electrons are taken to be arranged in concentric shells labelled K, L, M, N, O, etc., the K-shell being closest to the nucleus, the L-shell next, and so on (Fig. 20.3). The inner-shell electrons are tightly bound, and a large amount of energy is required to displace them from their normal energy levels. After such excitation, when the atom returns to its normal state, photons of large energy are emitted. Thus transitions of inner-shell electrons in heavy atoms give high energy photons, i.e. X-rays (Fig. 20.4, electromagnetic spectrum).

Characteristic X-rays: these X-rays consist of a series of specific wavelengths or frequencies, so they are called characteristic X-rays; their energies depend on the target element.

Importance: the study of characteristic X-ray spectra has played a very important role in the study of atomic structure and the periodic table of elements.

book_ref.quote: In heavy atoms, the electrons are assumed to be arranged in concentric shells

blocks.prompt: 10 A transition in a light atom emits a photon of 1.9 eV, while an inner-shell transition in a heavy atom emits a photon of 8.0 keV. Find the wavelength of each photon and the ratio of their energies (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert each energy to joules and use λ = hc/E; larger energy gives a much shorter wavelength.

book_ref.quote: Thus transition of inner shell electrons in heavy atoms gives rise to the emission of high energy photons or X-rays.

blocks.final_answer: 654 nm (visible light) and 1.55 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (X-ray); the X-ray photon has about 4.2 × 10³ times more energy.

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the production of X-rays in an X-ray tube and obtain the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons striking the target. Explain how Kα and Kβ X-rays are produced, write their energy equations, and explain why they are called characteristic X-rays. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
X-ray tube (Fig. 20.5): a high vacuum tube. The cathode C is heated by the filament F and emits electrons, which are accelerated towards the anode (target) T by a potential difference V between C and T.

Maximum kinetic energy: an electron of charge e accelerated through potential difference V gains energy Ve, so the maximum kinetic energy with which it strikes the target is
(K.E.)max = Ve ... (20.1)

Kα X-rays: the fast electrons of energy Ve strike a target of tungsten or another heavy element. In a collision, an electron in an innermost shell such as K or L may be knocked out. Suppose a K-shell electron is removed, leaving a vacancy (hole) in the K-shell. An electron from the L-shell jumps to fill it and emits a photon of energy hf, the Kα X-ray:
hf(Kα) = E_L − E_K ... (20.2)

Kβ X-rays: an electron from the M-shell may instead jump into the K-shell hole. The photons emitted in this M → K transition are Kβ X-rays:
hf(Kβ) = E_M − E_K ... (20.3)
Transitions from still higher shells give further K lines, and so on. The holes left in the L and M shells are filled by electrons from higher states, giving more X-rays.

Characteristic X-rays: photons from such inner-shell transitions are called characteristic X-rays because their energies depend upon the type of target material. They appear as discrete lines on a continuous spectrum (Fig. 20.6).

book_ref.quote: Fig. 20.5 shows an arrangement of producing X-rays.

blocks.prompt: 12 In a heavy target atom the energy levels are E_K = −69.5 keV, E_L = −11.0 keV and E_M = −2.5 keV. Find the energy (in joules) and the wavelength of (i) the Kα photon (ii) the Kβ photon (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use hf(Kα) = E_L − E_K and hf(Kβ) = E_M − E_K, convert keV to joules, then λ = hc/E.

book_ref.quote: The electron from the L-shell jumps to occupy the hole in the K-shell

blocks.final_answer: (i) Kα: 9.36 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, 2.13 × 10⁻¹¹ m (ii) Kβ: 1.07 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, 1.86 × 10⁻¹¹ m; Kβ has the higher energy and shorter wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain the origin of the continuous X-ray spectrum (bremsstrahlung). Why does it lie in the X-ray region? Show that the spectrum has a minimum wavelength and obtain its value in terms of the accelerating potential difference V. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Origin: the continuous spectrum is due to bremsstrahlung, or braking radiation. When the fast moving electrons bombard the target, they are suddenly slowed down on impact. An accelerating charge emits electromagnetic radiation, so these electrons emit radiation as they are strongly decelerated by the target.

X-ray region: since the rate of deceleration is so large, the emitted radiation has short wavelength, so the bremsstrahlung is in the X-ray region.

Minimum wavelength: an electron accelerated through V strikes the target with (K.E.)max = Ve. If an electron loses all its kinetic energy in the first collision, the entire kinetic energy appears as one X-ray photon of the largest frequency f_max:
(K.E.)max = hf_max, i.e. Ve = hf_max
Since c = f λ, the largest frequency corresponds to the smallest wavelength λmin (Fig. 20.6):
Ve = hc/λmin, so λmin = hc/(Ve)
No photon can have more energy than Ve, so no wavelength shorter than λmin is emitted.

The rest of the spectrum: other electrons do not lose all their energy in the first collision; they suffer a number of collisions before coming to rest, giving photons of smaller energy, i.e. X-rays of longer wavelength. Thus the continuous spectrum is obtained due to deceleration of the impacting electrons, with characteristic lines on top of it.

book_ref.quote: When the fast moving electrons bombard the target, they are suddenly slowed down on impact with the target.

blocks.prompt: 14 An X-ray tube is operated at 35 kV. Find (i) the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons striking the target (ii) the maximum frequency (iii) the minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: An electron that gives all its energy Ve to one photon produces f_max and λmin: Ve = hf_max = hc/λmin.

book_ref.quote: the entire kinetic energy appears as a X-ray photon

blocks.prompt: 15 What is attenuation of X-rays? Write the attenuation law and explain its terms. Explain contrast in X-ray images, the use of hard and soft X-rays and of contrast media, and the role of image intensifiers. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Attenuation: as X-rays travel through the body they lose energy because they interact with atoms. X-rays can ionize atoms, i.e. knock out electrons, which is how energy is transferred. This loss is called attenuation.

Attenuation law: the intensity of the beam decreases gradually as it passes through a material, following an exponential pattern:
I = I₀e^(−μx)
where I₀ = initial intensity, I = intensity after passing through the material, x = thickness of the material (in metres), and μ = attenuation coefficient, which depends on the material and the X-ray energy. The thickness x appears only in the exponent.

Contrast: contrast in X-ray images means how clearly we can tell different tissues apart; tissues that attenuate differently give different intensities on the image. Contrast depends on the X-ray energy:
• Hard X-rays (high energy) are used for bone imaging.
• Soft X-rays (low energy) are better for soft tissues such as the breast.

Contrast media: special substances such as iodine (Z = 53) or barium (Z = 56) that absorb X-rays well. They are injected or swallowed to highlight certain parts of the body; because of their high atomic numbers they increase X-ray absorption and make those tissues stand out more clearly.

Image intensifiers: used in real-time X-ray imaging (fluoroscopy); they brighten the image, making it easier to see, and so help reduce radiation exposure.

book_ref.quote: The intensity of the X-ray beam decreases gradually as it passes through a material.

blocks.prompt: 16 An X-ray beam passes through a tissue of attenuation coefficient 60 m⁻¹. Using I = I₀e^(−μx), find (i) the fraction of the intensity that emerges from a 2.0 cm thickness (ii) the thickness that reduces the intensity to half. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put x in metres into I/I₀ = e^(−μx); for half intensity set e^(−μx) = 1/2, so x = ln 2/μ.

book_ref.quote: x = thickness of the material (in metres)

blocks.final_answer: (i) 0.30 (about 30%) emerges (ii) about 1.2 cm halves the intensity.

blocks.prompt: 17 What is computed tomography? Explain the limitation of an ordinary X-ray image and describe how a CT scanner produces cross-sectional and three-dimensional images. Explain the name Computed Axial Tomography and give the advantages and the main risk of CT. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: computed tomography (CT) is a medical imaging technique that combines X-ray technology with computer processing to give high-resolution cross-sectional and 3D images of internal body structures. It is used for diagnosing diseases, detecting internal injuries and guiding treatment.

Limitation of an ordinary X-ray: it shows a flat (2D) image in which bones and organs overlap, so individual structures are hard to see; e.g. the front and back ribs appear on top of each other (Fig. 20.7).

Working: the X-ray tube rotates around the patient while the detectors stay in place, collecting information from all sides (Fig. 20.8). Many X-ray images of the same body section are taken from different angles, and a computer combines them into a detailed cross-sectional (slice) image. The scanner then moves slightly along the body and repeats the process for the next slice. Finally the computer combines all the slices, like stacking layers of a cake, into a 3D image (Fig. 20.9).

Name: Computed: a computer controls the scan, processes the data and converts it into images. Axial: the scan is taken along the body's axis. Tomography: from the Greek tomos, meaning slice, as the body is imaged layer by layer.

Advantages: CT shows the size, shape and exact location of organs, bones and other structures in three dimensions and distinguishes tissues even of very similar densities; e.g. it shows the position and size of a tumor so that it can be targeted accurately with high-energy X-rays or gamma rays.

Risk: CT exposes the patient to X-rays, a form of ionizing radiation, which carries a small risk; special precautions are taken, especially for pregnant women and patients with existing health concerns.

book_ref.quote: An ordinary X-ray shows a flat (2D) image of the body

blocks.prompt: 18 In one projection of a CT scan, an X-ray beam crosses 3.0 cm of soft tissue (μ = 20 m⁻¹) along one path and 3.0 cm of bone (μ = 50 m⁻¹) along another. Using I = I₀e^(−μx), find the fraction of the intensity reaching the detector along each path and the ratio of the two intensities. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Each path follows I/I₀ = e^(−μx); the difference between the two detector readings is what lets the computer tell the tissues apart.

book_ref.quote: This makes it easier to distinguish between tissues, even when they have very similar densities.

blocks.final_answer: About 55% passes through the soft tissue and 22% through the bone; the soft-tissue path delivers about 2.5 times more intensity.

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain the principle of nuclear medicine imaging and the SPECT technique. Describe the working of a PET scan, from the injection of the tracer to the formation of the image, and give its medical importance. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: imaging methods using ionizing radiation rely on how radiation interacts with matter: photons passing through tissue may be absorbed or scattered, and the pattern of energy deposition and attenuation gives measurable signals at a detector. In nuclear medicine the radiation originates inside the patient from an administered radiopharmaceutical, so the signal reflects physiological function rather than only anatomy.

SPECT: in Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography a gamma-emitting tracer is introduced into the body and a rotating gamma camera records many projection views; these are reconstructed into cross-sectional images of tracer distribution, giving 3D information about perfusion and organ function.

PET (Fig. 20.10, 20.11): PET extends this idea using positron-emitting tracers.
(i) A small amount of radioactive tracer is injected into a vein. The blood carries it, and it builds up more in very active tissues, such as many cancers or working parts of the brain and heart.
(ii) The unstable nuclei of the tracer decay and emit positrons. Each positron travels only a short distance before meeting an electron in nearby tissue.
(iii) The positron and electron annihilate; their mass is converted into energy as two gamma-ray photons moving in nearly opposite directions.
(iv) Detectors arranged in a ring around the patient detect these photon pairs in coincidence, which localizes each event, and send signals to a computer.
(v) The computer reconstructs a quantitative map of tracer uptake. Brighter areas mean higher tracer concentration and therefore higher tissue activity.

Importance: PET is a non-invasive technique that images metabolic and biochemical activity at the cellular/molecular level, so it is valuable for early cancer detection and staging, evaluating brain function and identifying cardiac abnormalities before clear anatomical changes appear.

book_ref.quote: In nuclear medicine, the radiation originates inside the patient

blocks.prompt: 20 In a PET scan a positron and an electron, each of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, annihilate at rest and produce two gamma photons of equal energy. Find (i) the energy of each photon in joules and in MeV (ii) its frequency (iii) its wavelength (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The mass of both particles becomes the energy of two equal photons, so each photon carries the energy mc² of one particle's mass.

book_ref.quote: When they meet, the positron and electron annihilate and their mass is converted into energy

blocks.final_answer: (i) 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J ≈ 0.512 MeV (ii) 1.24 × 10²⁰ Hz (iii) 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m, a gamma ray.
